item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Why would they even need a self-professed cannibal to confirm what kind of meat it is? We have science for that.

As mentioned, they didn't want to waste the science on a mostly-harmless SCP, they had the cannibal on hand, and they figured any weird-tasting magically-appearing meat just had to be human, so they went to him first. They only brought out the science once the easier method they had on hand failed.

Before even reaching the meat part, I was expecting this to be contained as part of a conspiracy to keep McDonalds and Burger King and other fast food chains in business, as a service providing quality food at lower prices than competitors with an instant delivery via "poofing" is sure to utterly destroy them.

The Foundation has no idea how the "poofing" part of the delivery is working at all - that alone made them want to secure it. Competition with other fast food business could be an issue too, although they haven't seen enough menus in the wild to be too worried about that.

Also general question I think of: It uses meat of commonly known endangered animals. How does it distinguish with regards to misconceptions, such as public belief that a certain animal is endangered when it's not, or belief that a certain animal isn't endangered when it is? Also, which public, where, and when? I doubt that the population of one city in Japan or South Korea will have the same "common knowledge" of endangered animals as a rural village in South America or Scandinavia.

The menus are always in English (North American English at that), and have only been picked up in the United States, so the common knowledge is pulled mainly from the population of the USA. As for content, it always picks something that's both on the EEC Endangered Species List and that the public would consider endangered. If the animal either isn't on the EEC list, or if no one really knows about the animal being on the list, then the menu won't pick it.

The menu itself causes no compulsion to use it over other fast food menus in double-blind testing, and has shown no ability to teleport or reproduce when left alone.

This doesn't seem entirely necessary; I like the genre-awareness in "Yes, we checked, it's not people. It's usually people meat but this time it's not", but that sentence there would make as much sense as saying that it most certainly does not smell like cinnamon.

Due to the lack of memetic effects or mobility from SCP-971, this SCP is considered Safe and requires only minimal containment procedures.

I'm not much of a fan of this sentence either. It seems self-evident.

as scanned and printed copies of SCP-971 have the full powers of the original

I wasn't aware that pieces of paper could have "powers". Perhaps "… as scanned and printed copies of SCP-971 share the same anomalous properties of the original" would be a better replacement.

On the whole, though, I like this. It's amusing.
